decks.title: Retirement and Death of a Partner — Part 1: Ratios, Goodwill, Revaluation and Reserves
goals: Calculate the new ratio and the gaining ratio when a partner retires or dies
Adjust the outgoing partner’s share of goodwill under Accounting Standard 26
Prepare the Revaluation Account and distribute reserves and accumulated profits or losses

slides.heading: Retirement and Death of a Partner
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **new and gaining ratios**, **goodwill**, **revaluation** and **reserves** when a partner leaves the firm.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: new and gaining ratios, goodwill under Accounting Standard 26, revaluation of assets and liabilities, and reserves and accumulated profits
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: When a partner retires or dies, the old partnership ends but the firm usually carries on. The partners who remain must work out their new shares, pay the outgoing partner for his share of goodwill, revalue the assets and liabilities, and share out past reserves. In this part we learn each of these adjustments, step by step, using one imagined firm.

slides.heading: Retirement and death: one set of adjustments
columns:
**Retirement**

- A partner leaves by notice or agreement.
- Usually at the end of the year.
- Paid to the **retiring partner**.

**Death**

- Can happen on any day.
- Profit **till the date of death** is added.
- Paid to his **executor**.

rows: A partner leaves by choice, with notice or by agreement
A partner dies; the firm usually continues under the deed
Usually the end of the accounting year
Share of profit from the start of the year to the date of death
New and gaining ratios, goodwill, revaluation, reserves, settlement

visual.alt: Table comparing retirement and death: retirement is by choice and usually at the year end, with payment to the retiring partner; death can occur on any day, payment goes to the executor, and the share of profit till the date of death must be added; ratios, goodwill, revaluation, reserves and settlement are common to both

slides.narration: Retirement and death look different, but the accounting is almost the same. In both, a partner leaves and the others continue. The only extra step on death is the share of profit from the start of the year to the date of death, and the money is paid to the executor, who is the legal representative of the partner who has died.

slides.heading: What has to be settled

nodes.label: 2. Goodwill: outgoing share credited, gaining partners debited
4. Reserves and accumulated profits or losses
5. Amount due: paid, or kept as a loan
6. Balance sheet of the reconstituted firm

visual.alt: Flow of the six adjustments on retirement or death: ratios, goodwill, revaluation, reserves, amount due and settlement, and the new balance sheet
visual.caption: Do the adjustments in this order

slides.narration: Here is the order we will follow. First the new ratio and the gaining ratio. Then goodwill, because the continuing partners will enjoy the outgoing partner’s share of future profits. Then revaluation and reserves, which belong to all the old partners. Their total gives the amount due. Finally the outgoing partner is paid or his money is kept as a loan, and a new balance sheet is drawn up.

slides.heading: Finding the new ratio and the gaining ratio
bullets: **Gain = new share − old share.**
The gains of the continuing partners add up to the outgoing partner’s share.

headers: New share of a continuing partner
rows: Old ratio between the continuing partners
New share − old share of each
Outgoing share taken in a stated proportion
The proportion in which they acquire

visual.alt: Table of three cases for the new ratio: if nothing is agreed, the continuing partners keep their old ratio and gain in that ratio; if a new ratio is agreed, gain is new share minus old share; if the outgoing share is taken in a stated proportion, new share is old share plus the portion acquired

slides.narration: The gaining ratio is the ratio in which the continuing partners take over the outgoing share. For each partner, subtract the old share from the new share. If nothing is agreed, they keep their old ratio and gain in that same ratio. If a new ratio is agreed, or the outgoing share is bought in a stated proportion, work out each gain separately.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: Sitara Traders
slides.body_md: An imagined firm in Jaipur: **Arjun, Bela and Chirag** share profits **5:3:2**. Chirag retires on 31 March 2026. Find the gaining ratio (a) if nothing is agreed, (b) if Arjun and Bela agree on **3:2**.
bullets: (a) Old ratio continues: new ratio 5:3, gaining ratio **5:3**.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 1: Arjun old one half, new three fifths, gain one tenth; Bela old three tenths, new two fifths, gain one tenth; Chirag retires giving up one fifth; the gaining ratio is one to one
visual.caption: With no agreement the new ratio would be 5:3 and the gaining ratio 5:3; with 3:2 agreed it is 1:1.

slides.narration: In case a, nothing is agreed, so Arjun and Bela simply continue five to three, and they gain in that same ratio. In case b they agree on three to two. Arjun's new share of three fifths minus his old one half gives one tenth. Bela's two fifths minus three tenths also gives one tenth. So the gaining ratio is one to one, not five to three.

visual.alt: Two bars of equal length showing the whole profit. Before: Arjun one half, Bela three tenths, Chirag one fifth. After Chirag retires: Arjun three fifths and Bela two fifths. Each continuing partner gains one tenth
visual.caption: The whole profit is always 1: the outgoing share is spread over the continuing partners.

slides.narration: Think of the whole profit as one bar. Before retirement, Arjun has half the bar, Bela three tenths and Chirag one fifth. After Chirag leaves, the same bar is divided only between Arjun and Bela. Chirag’s fifth has not vanished. It has been spread over the continuing partners, one tenth each in our example. That is exactly what the gaining ratio measures.

slides.heading: Quick check: one partner takes over
slides.body_md: Only one continuing partner takes over the outgoing share.
slides.narration: Add the outgoing share to the partner who takes it over. The other partner’s share does not change.

slides.heading: Sacrificing ratio and gaining ratio
columns:
**Sacrificing ratio**

- Old share − new share.
- Mainly on **admission**.

**Gaining ratio**

- New share − old share.
- Mainly on **retirement and death**.

rows: Retirement or death of a partner

visual.alt: Table comparing sacrificing ratio, old share minus new share, used on admission with the new partner paying for goodwill, and gaining ratio, new share minus old share, used on retirement or death with the gaining partners paying for goodwill

slides.narration: You met the sacrificing ratio on admission, when old partners give up part of their shares to a new partner. The gaining ratio is its mirror image. On retirement or death, the continuing partners gain, and they pay for what they gain. Remember the formulas: sacrifice is old minus new, gain is new minus old.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a share bought in a stated proportion
slides.body_md: An imagined firm in Gangtok: **Riya, Sahil and Tenzin** share profits **4:3:2**. Tenzin retires; Riya and Sahil take over his share **equally**.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 2: Riya and Sahil each acquire half of Tenzin’s two ninths, that is one ninth each; Riya’s new share is five ninths and Sahil’s four ninths
visual.caption: New ratio 5:4; gaining ratio 1:1.

slides.narration: Tenzin's share is two ninths. Riya and Sahil each take half of it, which is one ninth each. Riya's new share is four ninths plus one ninth, five ninths. Sahil's is three ninths plus one ninth, four ninths. So the new ratio is five to four, while the gaining ratio is one to one, because they acquired equal portions.

slides.heading: Quick check: is the gaining ratio always the old ratio?
slides.body_md: Think back to worked example 1, part (b).
slides.narration: Compare the old ratio five to three with the gaining ratio when three to two was agreed.

slides.heading: Goodwill on retirement or death (AS 26)
bullets: No Goodwill Account is raised: only **purchased goodwill** may be recorded.
Gaining partners **Dr**, outgoing partner **Cr**, in the **gaining ratio**.

nodes.label: Outgoing partner's share = value × his old share
Debit gaining partners in the gaining ratio

visual.alt: Flow of the goodwill adjustment: value the firm’s goodwill, find the outgoing partner’s share, debit the gaining partners in their gaining ratio and credit the outgoing partner’s capital account
visual.caption: No Goodwill Account is raised (AS 26)

slides.narration: The outgoing partner helped build the firm’s reputation, and the continuing partners will now enjoy his share of future profits. So they must pay him for his share of goodwill. Under Accounting Standard twenty-six, self-generated goodwill cannot be shown in the books. Instead, the gaining partners’ capital accounts are debited and the outgoing partner’s capital account is credited.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: goodwill at Sitara Traders
slides.body_md: Goodwill of the firm is valued at **₹1,80,000**. Chirag's share = 1,80,000 × 1/5 = **₹36,000**. Arjun and Bela gain 1:1.

rows: *(Being Chirag's share of goodwill adjusted in the gaining ratio 1:1)*

visual.alt: Journal entry: Arjun's capital debited 18,000 and Bela's capital debited 18,000, Chirag's capital credited 36,000

slides.narration: The firm's goodwill is worth rupees one lakh eighty thousand. Chirag owned one fifth of it, which is rupees thirty-six thousand. Arjun and Bela gain equally, so each is debited rupees eighteen thousand, and Chirag's capital account is credited with the full rupees thirty-six thousand. Notice that no goodwill account appears anywhere in this entry.

slides.heading: Goodwill already in the books
bullets: Write it off **first**, among **all** partners in the **old ratio**.
Then adjust the outgoing share at the **current** value.

rows: *(Being existing goodwill written off in the old ratio 5:3:2)*

visual.alt: Journal entry writing off existing goodwill of 30,000: Arjun 15,000, Bela 9,000 and Chirag 6,000 debited

slides.narration: Sitara Traders already shows goodwill of rupees thirty thousand in its books. This old figure belongs to all three partners, so it is written off in the old ratio of five to three to two, including Chirag. Only after that do we make the fresh goodwill adjustment at today's value. Doing both steps avoids counting goodwill twice.

slides.heading: Quick check: old goodwill
slides.body_md: Who bears the write-off, and in which ratio?
slides.narration: The old goodwill was built by the old firm. Which partners, and which ratio?

slides.heading: The Revaluation Account

rows: Decrease in the value of an asset
Increase in the value of an asset
Balance: profit to all partners (old ratio)
Balance: loss to all partners (old ratio)

visual.alt: Format of the Revaluation Account: losses on the debit side, such as a fall in an asset, a rise in a liability, an unrecorded liability or a new provision; gains on the credit side, such as a rise in an asset, a fall in a liability or an unrecorded asset; the balance is profit or loss shared by all partners in the old ratio

slides.narration: Assets and liabilities are revalued so that the outgoing partner gets his fair share of any gain or bears his share of any loss. Losses go on the debit side and gains on the credit side of the Revaluation Account. The balance is a profit or loss that belongs to all the partners, including the outgoing one, in the old ratio.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: revaluation at Sitara Traders
slides.body_md: Building up ₹40,000; stock down ₹8,000; provision for doubtful debts 5% on debtors of ₹60,000; an unrecorded repair bill of ₹4,000.

rows: To Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c

visual.alt: Revaluation Account of Sitara Traders: losses of stock 8,000, provision 3,000 and repair bill 4,000 on the debit side; building gain 40,000 on the credit side; profit 25,000 shared 12,500, 7,500 and 5,000
visual.caption: Profit on revaluation ₹25,000.

slides.narration: The building gains rupees forty thousand, a credit. Stock falls by rupees eight thousand, a five per cent provision on debtors costs rupees three thousand, and the unrecorded repair bill adds rupees four thousand; all three are debits. The net profit is rupees twenty-five thousand, shared five to three to two: rupees twelve thousand five hundred, rupees seven thousand five hundred and rupees five thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: debit or credit?
slides.body_md: Fill in both blanks.
slides.narration: Ask yourself whether each change is a gain or a loss for the old partners.

slides.heading: Reserves and accumulated profits

rows: General Reserve; Profit and Loss (credit balance)
Credited to all partners in the old ratio
Debited to all partners in the old ratio
Claim first; the surplus to all partners in the old ratio; an excess claim is a revaluation loss
Fall in value first; the balance to all partners in the old ratio

visual.alt: Table of reserves and accumulated profits: general reserve and a credit balance of profit and loss are credited to all partners in the old ratio; a debit balance is debited to them; the workmen compensation reserve first meets the claim and the investment fluctuation reserve first meets the fall in value, with the balance distributed

slides.narration: Reserves and undistributed profits were earned while the outgoing partner was a member, so they are shared by all the partners in the old ratio. An accumulated loss is shared the same way. Two reserves need care: the workmen compensation reserve must first cover the expected claim, and the investment fluctuation reserve must first absorb any fall in the value of investments.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: reserves at Sitara Traders
slides.body_md: General Reserve ₹50,000; Workmen Compensation Reserve ₹20,000 with an expected claim of ₹12,000.

rows: *(Being general reserve distributed in the old ratio)*
*(Being claim provided; surplus reserve distributed in the old ratio)*

visual.alt: Journal entries: general reserve of 50,000 credited to Arjun, Bela and Chirag in the old ratio; workmen compensation reserve of 20,000 debited, claim of 12,000 provided and the surplus of 8,000 credited to the partners

slides.narration: The general reserve of rupees fifty thousand is credited to all three partners, five to three to two. From the workmen compensation reserve of rupees twenty thousand, the expected claim of rupees twelve thousand becomes a liability, and only the surplus of rupees eight thousand is shared among the partners.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: New share − old share of each continuing partner
Gaining partners Dr; outgoing partner Cr
All partners Dr; Goodwill A/c Cr
All partners, including the outgoing one

visual.alt: Summary table: the outgoing partner’s goodwill is adjusted in the gaining ratio, debiting the gaining partners; existing goodwill, revaluation results, reserves and accumulated profits or losses are all shared in the old ratio by all partners, including the outgoing one

slides.narration: To sum up: gain equals new share minus old share. The outgoing partner’s goodwill is paid for by the gaining partners in the gaining ratio, and no goodwill account is raised. Old goodwill, revaluation results, reserves and accumulated profits or losses all belong to the old firm, so they are shared by every partner, including the outgoing one, in the old ratio.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always show the **gaining ratio working** (new − old) before the goodwill entry.
If a continuing partner’s share **falls**, credit him too: he sacrifices.
Write off **existing goodwill** in the **old ratio** before the fresh adjustment.
Revaluation, reserves and accumulated losses: **all partners, old ratio**.
Workmen compensation reserve: **claim first**, surplus to partners; an excess claim is a revaluation loss.
slides.narration: Some advice for the board exam. Show the gaining ratio working, because examiners give marks for it. Watch for a continuing partner whose share goes down; he must be credited for goodwill. Never use the new ratio for revaluation or reserves. And for the workmen compensation reserve, always deal with the claim first.

decks.title: Retirement and Death of a Partner — Part 2: Settlement, Loan, Balance Sheet and Death
goals: Prepare the capital accounts and find the amount due to the outgoing partner
Prepare the retiring partner’s loan account and the balance sheet of the reconstituted firm
Adjust continuing partners’ capitals to the new ratio
Calculate a deceased partner’s profit till death and prepare the executor’s account

slides.heading: Settling the account of an outgoing partner
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the **amount due**, **payment and loan**, the **new balance sheet**, **capital adjustment**, and the **death** of a partner.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: amount due, payment and loan account, balance sheet, capital adjustment, then the death of a partner with profit till death and the executor’s account
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In part one we made every adjustment. Now we bring them together. We find how much the firm owes the outgoing partner, decide how he is paid, prepare his loan account and the new balance sheet, and adjust the capitals of the partners who remain. Finally we deal with the death of a partner, which adds one more calculation and an executor’s account.

slides.heading: The amount due to the outgoing partner

headers: Credited to the outgoing partner's capital
Debited to the outgoing partner's capital
rows: Opening capital (and current account credit balance)
Share of goodwill from the gaining partners
Share of goodwill written off, if it was in the books
Share of reserves and accumulated profits
Interest on capital, salary, commission, profit till death (if any)

visual.alt: Table of what goes into the outgoing partner's capital account: credits are opening capital, goodwill from gaining partners, revaluation profit, reserves and any interest, salary or profit till death; debits are drawings, goodwill written off, revaluation loss, accumulated losses and interest on drawings
visual.caption: Balance of the capital account = amount due.

slides.narration: Everything the firm owes the outgoing partner is collected in his capital account. On the credit side go his capital, his share of goodwill, revaluation profit and reserves. On the debit side go his drawings and his share of losses. The balance of the account, after all the adjustments, is the amount due to him.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: capital accounts at Sitara Traders
slides.body_md: Using worked examples 3 to 5: Chirag is paid **₹46,600** by bank and the rest is left as a **loan**.

visual.alt: Partners' capital accounts of Sitara Traders: Chirag's account closes with 46,600 paid by bank and 1,00,000 transferred to his loan; Arjun and Bela carry down 2,08,500 and 1,47,900
visual.caption: Amount due to Chirag ₹1,46,600.

slides.narration: Chirag's account starts with rupees one lakh. Add revaluation profit, reserves and his goodwill of rupees thirty-six thousand from Arjun and Bela, and subtract his share of the old goodwill written off. The amount due is rupees one lakh forty-six thousand six hundred. He takes rupees forty-six thousand six hundred now, and rupees one lakh is transferred to his loan account. Arjun and Bela carry down their new balances.

slides.heading: How the outgoing partner is paid
bullets: If the firm and the partner agree nothing about interest, **Section 37** of the Indian Partnership Act 1932 gives him, at his option, **interest at 6% per annum** or the share of profit earned with his money.

rows: Retiring Partner's Capital A/c Dr, To Bank A/c
Retiring Partner's Capital A/c Dr, To Retiring Partner's Loan A/c
Interest A/c Dr, To Retiring Partner's Loan A/c
Rate as agreed; Section 37 if nothing is agreed
Retiring Partner's Loan A/c Dr, To Bank A/c

visual.alt: Table of modes of payment: paying at once through the bank, leaving the amount as a loan shown as a liability, crediting interest to the loan, and paying instalments from the loan account

slides.narration: The firm may pay the whole amount at once, or keep it as a loan and repay it in instalments with interest. The loan is a liability of the firm. If nothing has been agreed, the Partnership Act lets the outgoing partner choose between interest at six per cent a year and the share of profit earned with his money.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the entries
slides.body_md: Match each event with its journal entry.
slides.narration: Look at which account is being closed, which is being reduced, and which one grows.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: Chirag’s loan account
slides.body_md: ₹1,00,000 is repaid in **two equal yearly instalments** on 31 March 2027 and 2028, with interest at **10% per annum** on the unpaid balance.

visual.alt: Chirag's loan account: 1,00,000 on 31 March 2026; interest 10,000 and payment 60,000 in the first year; interest 5,000 and payment 55,000 in the second year, when the loan is closed
visual.caption: Interest is on the opening balance of each year.

slides.narration: Each instalment of principal is rupees fifty thousand. In the first year interest is ten per cent of rupees one lakh, that is rupees ten thousand, so the firm pays rupees sixty thousand. In the second year interest is only on the remaining rupees fifty thousand, so the payment is rupees fifty-five thousand, and the loan is closed.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: the new balance sheet
slides.body_md: Balance sheet of Arjun and Bela as at 31 March 2026, after Chirag’s retirement.
bullets: Assets at **revalued** figures; new liabilities (repair bill, claim) included.
Reserves are gone (distributed); Chirag's loan appears as a **liability**.

visual.alt: Balance sheet of Arjun and Bela after Chirag's retirement, totalling 5,42,400 on each side, with Chirag's loan of 1,00,000 as a liability
visual.caption: Revalued figures; the reserves have gone to the capitals.

slides.narration: Now redraw the balance sheet. Assets appear at their revalued figures, and debtors are shown net of the new provision. The repair bill and the workmen's claim are new liabilities. The reserves have disappeared because they went into the capitals. Chirag's loan of rupees one lakh is a liability. Both sides total rupees five lakh forty-two thousand four hundred.

slides.heading: Quick check: interest on a loan
slides.body_md: Interest is on the balance **outstanding** in that year.
slides.narration: First find how much of the loan is still unpaid at the start of the second year.

slides.heading: Adjusting the continuing partners’ capitals

nodes.label: Total capital of the new firm
Bring in the deficit or withdraw the surplus

visual.alt: Flow of capital adjustment: total capital times new share gives each required capital; compare with the adjusted capital and bring in or withdraw the difference
visual.caption: Or transfer the difference to current accounts

slides.narration: Sometimes the continuing partners agree to keep their capitals in their new profit-sharing ratio. Multiply the total capital of the new firm by each partner’s new share to get the required capital. A partner who has less brings in cash; a partner who has more withdraws it. Instead of cash, the difference can also go to current accounts.

slides.heading: Worked example 9: capital adjustment at Sitara Traders
slides.body_md: Arjun and Bela fix the total capital at **₹3,60,000** in their new ratio **3:2**.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 9: required capitals 2,16,000 and 1,44,000 against adjusted capitals 2,08,500 and 1,47,900; Arjun brings in 7,500 and Bela withdraws 3,900

slides.narration: Three fifths of rupees three lakh sixty thousand is rupees two lakh sixteen thousand, and two fifths is rupees one lakh forty-four thousand. Arjun has only rupees two lakh eight thousand five hundred, so he brings in rupees seven thousand five hundred. Bela has rupees one lakh forty-seven thousand nine hundred, which is rupees three thousand nine hundred more than needed, so she withdraws it.

slides.heading: Death of a partner: what is different

nodes.label: Profit from the start of the year to death

visual.alt: Flow on death: from the date of death, add the share of profit till death, make the usual adjustments, transfer the balance to the executor’s account, and pay it or keep it as a loan
visual.caption: Same steps as retirement, plus profit till death

slides.narration: When a partner dies, every adjustment you have learnt still applies. Two things change. Death can happen on any day, so his share of profit from the beginning of the year to the date of death must be calculated. And the amount due is paid not to him but to his executor, through an account called the executor’s account.

slides.heading: Profit till the date of death
slides.body_md: An imagined firm in Mysuru, **Kaveri Handlooms**: Meera, Nakul and Kabir share 2:2:1; books close on 31 March. Kabir dies on **30 June 2026**. Last year: profit ₹3,60,000 on sales of ₹24,00,000; profits of the last three years ₹2,70,000, ₹3,30,000, ₹4,50,000; sales from 1 April to 30 June ₹7,00,000.
bullets: **Time basis:** last year’s (or average) profit × months ÷ 12 × his share.
**Turnover basis:** last year’s rate of profit on sales × sales till death × his share.

rows: Sales till death × last year profit ÷ last year sales

visual.alt: Table of the bases for profit till death for an imagined firm: time basis on last year's profit gives 18,000, time basis on average profit gives 17,500, and the sales basis gives 21,000
visual.caption: The deed decides the basis; the time basis assumes profit accrues evenly.

slides.narration: Kabir, of the imagined Kaveri Handlooms, dies on thirtieth June, three months into the year. On last year's profit his share is rupees eighteen thousand. On the average profit of three years it is rupees seventeen thousand five hundred. On the sales basis, applying last year's profit rate to sales up to his death, it is rupees twenty-one thousand. The partnership deed says which basis to use.

slides.heading: Worked example 10: Profit and Loss Suspense
slides.body_md: The profit of the current year is not known yet, so the debit is **parked** in a suspense account.
bullets: If a balance sheet is drawn up on the date of death, the suspense balance appears on the **assets** side.

rows: Profit and Loss Suspense A/c Dr
*(Being Kabir's share of profit till death on the sales basis)*

visual.alt: Journal entry: Profit and Loss Suspense debited and Kabir's capital credited with 21,000

slides.narration: Kabir's share of rupees twenty-one thousand is credited to his capital account. The year's profit is not yet known, so the debit goes to Profit and Loss Suspense Account. When the year closes and profits are divided, this suspense balance is cleared. If a balance sheet is prepared on the date of death, it is shown on the assets side.

slides.heading: Quick check: the suspense entry
slides.body_md: Which account is debited, and which is credited?
slides.narration: The deceased partner is owed the profit. Which account records that the profit is not yet known?

slides.body_md: Kabir's capital ₹1,20,000; General Reserve ₹40,000; goodwill of the firm ₹1,50,000 (Meera and Nakul continue 1:1); drawings ₹9,000; profit till death on the sales basis.

notes.title: Retirement and Death of a Partner — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Retirement and death: what changes
sections.body_md:
A partner may **retire** (by notice, by agreement or under the deed) or **die**. The old partnership ends but the firm continues with the remaining partners. Because the outgoing partner was entitled to a share of profits, goodwill, revaluation results and reserves, the accounts must settle his claim.

**Adjustments, in order:**
1. New profit-sharing ratio and gaining ratio.
2. Goodwill (AS 26).
3. Revaluation of assets and reassessment of liabilities.
4. Reserves and accumulated profits or losses.
5. Amount due, and its payment (cash, loan, instalments).
6. Balance sheet of the reconstituted firm; capital adjustment if agreed.

On **death**, add the share of profit **till the date of death** and pay the amount to the **executor**.

A change in the agreement among partners, such as on retirement or death, while the firm continues.

sections.heading: 2. New ratio and gaining ratio
sections.body_md:
**Gain of a continuing partner = new share − old share.** The gains add up to the outgoing partner’s share.

- **Nothing agreed:** continuing partners keep their old ratio between themselves; gaining ratio = their old ratio.
- **New ratio agreed:** compute each gain separately; it may differ from the old ratio, and one partner may even **sacrifice**.
- **Outgoing share acquired in a stated proportion:** new share = old share + portion acquired; gaining ratio = the proportion of acquisition.

The gaining ratio is used for **goodwill** only. Revaluation and reserves always use the **old ratio**.

sections.heading: 3. Goodwill on retirement or death (AS 26)
sections.body_md:
Accounting Standard 26 allows only **purchased goodwill** to be recorded, so no Goodwill Account is raised at its full value. Instead:

- Outgoing partner’s share of goodwill = value of the firm’s goodwill × his old share.
- **Gaining partners’ Capital A/cs Dr** (in the gaining ratio), **To Outgoing Partner’s Capital A/c**.
- A continuing partner whose share **falls** is also credited for his sacrifice.
- **Existing goodwill** in the books is first **written off** among all partners in the **old ratio**: All Partners’ Capital A/cs Dr, To Goodwill A/c.

The goodwill may itself have to be valued first (average profit, super profit or capitalisation method, from Chapter 1).

sections.heading: 4. Revaluation, reserves and accumulated profits
sections.body_md:
**Revaluation Account:** debit decreases in assets, increases in liabilities, unrecorded liabilities and new provisions; credit increases in assets, decreases in liabilities and unrecorded assets. The balance is a profit (or loss) transferred to **all partners in the old ratio**.

**Reserves and accumulated profits** (General Reserve, credit balance of Profit and Loss, Contingency Reserve) are credited to all partners in the old ratio; an **accumulated loss** is debited the same way.

- **Workmen Compensation Reserve:** the claim is met first; the surplus goes to partners; an excess claim is debited to the Revaluation Account.
- **Investment Fluctuation Reserve:** the fall in the market value of investments is met first; the balance goes to partners.

sections.heading: 5. Settling the outgoing partner: capital and loan accounts
sections.body_md:
**Amount due** = balance of his capital account after all adjustments (capital, goodwill, revaluation, reserves, interest or salary due, profit till death; less drawings and losses).

**Settlement:**
- Paid at once: Capital A/c Dr, To Bank A/c.
- Kept in the firm: Capital A/c Dr, To **Loan A/c** (a liability).
- Interest each year: Interest A/c Dr, To Loan A/c.
- Each instalment: Loan A/c Dr, To Bank A/c.

Without an agreement, **Section 37** of the Indian Partnership Act 1932 lets him choose interest at **6% per annum** or the share of profit earned with his money.

sections.heading: 6. The new balance sheet and capital adjustment
sections.body_md:
**Balance sheet of the reconstituted firm:** assets and liabilities at revalued figures; unrecorded items brought in; reserves removed (distributed); the outgoing partner’s loan (if any) on the liabilities side; the continuing partners’ adjusted capitals.

**Capital adjustment (if agreed):**
1. Required capital = total capital of the new firm × new share.
2. Compare with the adjusted capital.
3. Deficit: Bank A/c Dr, To Partner’s Capital A/c. Surplus: Partner’s Capital A/c Dr, To Bank A/c (or to his Current A/c).

The total capital may be stated, or taken as the combined adjusted capitals of the continuing partners.

sections.heading: 7. Death: profit till the date of death and the executor’s account
sections.body_md:
**Share of profit till the date of death**
- **Time basis:** last year’s profit (or the average of some years) × months from the start of the year to death ÷ 12 × his share.
- **Turnover (sales) basis:** rate of profit = last year’s profit ÷ last year’s sales; profit till death = rate × sales up to death; × his share.

**Entry:** Profit and Loss Suspense A/c Dr, To Deceased Partner’s Capital A/c. (If a balance sheet is prepared on the date of death, the suspense balance is shown on the assets side.)

**Executor’s Account:** Deceased Partner’s Capital A/c Dr, To Executor’s A/c (amount due). The executor is paid at once or the balance is transferred to the Executor’s Loan A/c and paid with interest.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using the **old ratio** for goodwill when a new ratio is agreed: always compute **new − old**.
- Forgetting to credit a continuing partner whose share **falls**.
- Using the **new ratio** for revaluation, reserves or old goodwill (always the **old ratio**).
- Distributing the whole Workmen Compensation Reserve without providing for the **claim**.
- Charging loan interest on the original amount instead of the **opening balance** of each year.
- Crediting profit till death to the executor directly instead of to the **capital account**.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: correct option, ratio or entry.
- 3 marks: ratio working (1) + entries or account (2), or a profit-till-death calculation with its entry.
- 4 marks: a Revaluation Account, a loan account over the years, or a set of entries, with step marks.
- 6 marks: Revaluation Account + capital accounts + balance sheet (about 2 marks each), or capital and executor’s accounts.

questions.stem_md: On the retirement of a partner, the gain of each continuing partner is calculated as

options.text_md: his old share minus his new share
his new share minus his old share
the retiring partner's share divided equally among the continuing partners
his new share divided by his old share

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** his new share minus his old share. Gain = new share − old share. Old minus new is the sacrifice formula used on admission; an equal division is only a special case of agreement; a quotient of shares has no meaning here.

questions.stem_md: Rekha, Sunil and Tara run an imagined printing press in Sivakasi and share profits in the ratio 4:3:2. Tara retires, and nothing is agreed about the future ratio. The gaining ratio of Rekha and Sunil will be
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 4:3. With no agreement, the continuing partners keep their old ratio between themselves, so the new ratio is 4:3. Rekha gains 8/63 and Sunil gains 2/21, so the gaining ratio is 4:3, the same as their old ratio.

questions.stem_md: Om, Pallavi and Qadir, partners in an imagined courier firm in Lucknow, share profits 4:3:2. Qadir retires and his share is taken over by Om and Pallavi in the ratio 2:1. The new profit-sharing ratio of Om and Pallavi is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 16:11. Qadir's share is 2/9. Om takes 2/3 of it = 4/27 and Pallavi 1/3 of it = 2/27. New shares: Om 4/9 + 4/27 = 16/27; Pallavi 3/9 + 2/27 = 11/27. New ratio 16:11.

questions.stem_md: Nikhil, Mohan and Lata share the profits of an imagined dairy in Anand in the ratio 3:2:1. Lata retires, and Nikhil and Mohan agree to share future profits equally. Which statement about the gain is correct?

options.text_md: Nikhil and Mohan gain in the ratio 3:2
Nikhil and Mohan gain in the ratio 1:1
Only Mohan gains; he takes over Lata's whole share of 1/6
Nikhil gains 1/6 and Mohan gives up 1/6

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Only Mohan gains; he takes over Lata's whole share of 1/6. Nikhil: new 1/2 − old 1/2 = nil. Mohan: new 1/2 − old 1/3 = 1/6. So Mohan alone gains, and his gain equals Lata's share; only Mohan compensates Lata for goodwill.

questions.stem_md: Harsh, Isha and Jai share profits 2:2:1 in an imagined photo studio in Nashik. Jai retires and Isha alone takes over Jai's share. The new ratio of Harsh and Isha is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 2:3. Harsh keeps 2/5. Isha gets 2/5 + 1/5 = 3/5. New ratio 2:3; Isha alone is the gaining partner.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** On a partner's retirement, the continuing partners compensate him for his share of goodwill in their gaining ratio.

**Reason (R):** The continuing partners acquire the retiring partner's share of future profits in the gaining ratio.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. The continuing partners pay for goodwill because they take over his future profits, and they take them over in the gaining ratio; so R explains A.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Even when the continuing partners agree on a new profit-sharing ratio, their gaining ratio is always equal to their old ratio.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Gaining ratio equals the old ratio only when the continuing partners keep their old ratio between themselves. When a new ratio is agreed, each gain must be worked out as new share − old share, and it can differ from the old ratio.

questions.solution_md: Gain is the new share minus the old share.

**New share = old share + share acquired.**

questions.stem_md: Gauri, Hari and Ishaan share the profits of an imagined pottery studio in Khurja in the ratio 5:4:3. Ishaan retires. Gauri takes one-third of Ishaan's share and Hari takes the remaining two-thirds. Find the new profit-sharing ratio and the gaining ratio of Gauri and Hari.
questions.solution_md: Take the stated portion of the outgoing partner's share, add it to each old share, then compare.

answer.model_answer_md:
Ishaan's share = 3/12 = 1/4.

- Gauri acquires 1/3 × 1/4 = **1/12**; Hari acquires 2/3 × 1/4 = **1/6**.
- Gauri's new share = 5/12 + 1/12 = **1/2**.
- Hari's new share = 4/12 + 1/6 = **1/2**.

**New ratio = 1:1**; **gaining ratio = 1/12 : 1/6 = 1:2**.

Note: the partners end up equal even though they gain unequally.

| Formula | Old share − new share | New share − old share |
| When calculated | Mainly on the admission of a partner | Mainly on the retirement or death of a partner |
| Goodwill | The new partner compensates the sacrificing partners | The gaining partners compensate the outgoing partner |

questions.stem_md: Under Accounting Standard 26, the retiring partner's share of goodwill is adjusted by

options.text_md: crediting his capital account and debiting the continuing partners' capital accounts in their gaining ratio
debiting his capital account and crediting the continuing partners' capital accounts in their old ratio
raising a Goodwill Account at its full value and crediting all the partners
crediting the Revaluation Account with the retiring partner's share

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** crediting his capital account and debiting the continuing partners' capital accounts in their gaining ratio. Goodwill is not raised in the books. The gaining partners, who will enjoy the extra future profit, pay the retiring partner through their capital accounts in the gaining ratio.

questions.stem_md: Devika, Esha and Farid share profits 2:2:1 in an imagined pharmacy in Pune. Farid retires; the firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,50,000 and Devika and Esha will share future profits 3:2. The correct entry for goodwill is

options.text_md: Devika's Capital A/c Dr ₹15,000 and Esha's Capital A/c Dr ₹15,000, To Farid's Capital A/c ₹30,000
Goodwill A/c Dr ₹1,50,000, To all partners' capital accounts in 2:2:1
Farid's Capital A/c Dr ₹30,000, To Devika's Capital A/c ₹30,000
Devika's Capital A/c Dr ₹30,000, To Farid's Capital A/c ₹30,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Devika's Capital A/c Dr ₹30,000, To Farid's Capital A/c ₹30,000. Gains: Devika 3/5 − 2/5 = 1/5; Esha 2/5 − 2/5 = nil. Farid's share = 1/5 × 1,50,000 = 30,000, borne wholly by Devika, the only gaining partner.

questions.stem_md: Goodwill already appearing in the balance sheet when a partner retires is

options.text_md: written off among the continuing partners in their new ratio
written off among all the partners, including the retiring partner, in their old ratio
carried forward to the balance sheet of the reconstituted firm
credited to the retiring partner alone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** written off among all the partners, including the retiring partner, in their old ratio. The old goodwill belongs to the old firm, so all old partners write it off in the old ratio before the retiring partner is compensated for goodwill at its current value.

questions.stem_md: A profit on revaluation at the time of retirement is shared by

options.text_md: all the partners, including the retiring partner, in the old ratio
the continuing partners in their new ratio
the continuing partners in their gaining ratio
the retiring partner alone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** all the partners, including the retiring partner, in the old ratio. The change in values arose while all of them were partners, so the profit or loss is shared by all partners in the old ratio.

questions.stem_md: On the retirement of a partner, an asset that was never recorded in the books is brought in. It is

options.text_md: debited to the Revaluation Account as a loss
credited to the Revaluation Account as a gain
credited to the retiring partner's capital account only
ignored, because it was never recorded

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** credited to the Revaluation Account as a gain. Bringing in an unrecorded asset increases the value of the firm, a gain shared by all the old partners through the Revaluation Account.

questions.stem_md: The balance sheet of an imagined firm shows a Workmen Compensation Reserve of ₹30,000. On a partner's retirement, the workmen's claim is estimated at ₹36,000. The excess claim of ₹6,000 will be

options.text_md: credited to all the partners' capital accounts
debited to the retiring partner's capital account only
debited to the Revaluation Account
ignored, because a reserve already exists

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** debited to the Revaluation Account. The reserve covers 30,000 of the claim; the extra 6,000 is a new liability, a loss debited to the Revaluation Account and shared by all partners in the old ratio.

questions.stem_md: An imagined firm has an Investment Fluctuation Reserve of ₹20,000. On a partner's retirement, investments shown at ₹1,00,000 have a market value of ₹88,000. The treatment of the reserve is

options.text_md: the whole ₹20,000 goes to all partners in the old ratio
₹12,000 is debited to the Revaluation Account and the reserve is untouched
the remaining ₹8,000 goes to the continuing partners in their new ratio
₹12,000 of it absorbs the fall and the remaining ₹8,000 goes to all partners in the old ratio

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹12,000 of it absorbs the fall and the remaining ₹8,000 goes to all partners in the old ratio. The fall in value of 12,000 is met from the reserve; only the balance 8,000 is an accumulated profit, credited to all partners in the old ratio.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When a partner retires, no Goodwill Account is raised in the books at the firm's full goodwill.

**Reason (R):** Accounting Standard 26 allows goodwill to be recorded only when it is purchased for a consideration.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Self-generated goodwill cannot be recorded under AS 26, which is exactly why it is adjusted through the capital accounts instead; R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** On retirement, the general reserve is credited only to the continuing partners in their new ratio.

**Reason (R):** Reserves are past profits that belong to all the partners who were in the firm when they were set aside.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: the reserve goes to all partners, including the retiring one, in the old ratio. R is true and is the reason the retiring partner must get his share.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A debit balance of the Profit and Loss Account shown on the assets side at the time of retirement is debited to all the partners' capital accounts in their old ratio.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** An accumulated loss belongs to all old partners, so it is written off to every capital account, including the retiring partner, in the old ratio.

questions.stem_md: An increase in the value of an asset on revaluation is ___ to the Revaluation Account, and an unrecorded liability brought into the books is ___ to it.
questions.solution_md: A rise in an asset is a gain, so it is credited; a new liability is a loss, so it is debited.

questions.stem_md: Sara, Tanvir and Uma share profits 2:1:1. Uma retires and the goodwill of the imagined firm is valued at ₹2,40,000. How much will be credited to Uma's capital account for her share of goodwill (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md: Uma's share = 1/4. Her share of goodwill = 2,40,000 × 1/4 = 60,000. So ₹60,000 is credited to her capital account.

questions.stem_md: If the amount due to a retiring partner is not paid at once and there is no agreement on interest, Section 37 of the Indian Partnership Act 1932 entitles him to

options.text_md: interest at 12 per cent per annum in every case
nothing until the whole amount is paid
interest at 6 per cent per annum, payable only by the gaining partners personally
interest at 6 per cent per annum or the share of profit earned with his money, whichever he chooses

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** interest at 6 per cent per annum or the share of profit earned with his money, whichever he chooses. Section 37 gives the outgoing partner (or his estate) an option: interest at 6% per annum on the unpaid amount, or the share of profits attributable to the use of his money.

questions.stem_md: Zara retires and the whole amount due to her is to remain in the firm as a loan. The journal entry is

options.text_md: Zara's Loan A/c Dr, To Zara's Capital A/c
Zara's Capital A/c Dr, To Bank A/c
Zara's Capital A/c Dr, To Zara's Loan A/c
Bank A/c Dr, To Zara's Loan A/c

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Zara's Capital A/c Dr, To Zara's Loan A/c. Her capital account is closed by a debit, and the firm now owes her the same amount as a loan, a liability credited to her loan account.

questions.stem_md: A retiring partner's loan of ₹1,80,000 is repaid in three equal yearly instalments of principal, together with interest at 10% per annum on the amount outstanding. The total paid at the end of the second year is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹72,000. Instalment = 1,80,000 ÷ 3 = 60,000. In year 2 the outstanding loan is 1,20,000, so interest = 12,000; total 72,000.

questions.stem_md: When the continuing partners agree to keep their capitals in their new profit-sharing ratio, each partner's required capital is found as

options.text_md: the total capital of the new firm multiplied by his new share
his adjusted capital multiplied by his gain
the total capital of the new firm divided equally among the partners
the retiring partner's capital multiplied by his old share

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the total capital of the new firm multiplied by his new share. Required capital = total capital × new share; the difference from the adjusted capital is brought in or withdrawn (or taken to the current account).

questions.stem_md: After a partner retires, the adjusted capitals of Varun and Wahida are ₹1,30,000 and ₹70,000. The total capital of the reconstituted firm is to be ₹2,40,000 in their new ratio 3:1, any surplus or deficit being settled in cash. Which is correct?

options.text_md: Varun brings in ₹40,000 and Wahida brings in nothing
Varun brings in ₹50,000 and Wahida withdraws ₹10,000
Each partner brings in ₹20,000
Varun withdraws ₹50,000 and Wahida brings in ₹10,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Varun brings in ₹50,000 and Wahida withdraws ₹10,000. Required capitals: Varun 3/4 × 2,40,000 = 1,80,000; Wahida 1/4 × 2,40,000 = 60,000. Varun is short by 50,000; Wahida has 10,000 more than needed.

**Reason (R):** Interest on a retiring partner's loan is a charge against the profits of the firm.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R is about how the interest is treated later; it does not explain why the unpaid amount becomes a loan (he has ceased to be a partner and is now a creditor).

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The firm owes the money to the retiring partner, so his loan is a liability, shown on the liabilities side until it is repaid.

Qasim, Radha and Sanjay share profits 2:2:1 in an imagined auto-parts firm in Faridabad. Sanjay dies on 30 June 2026; the books close on 31 March. His capital is ₹1,00,000, the General Reserve is ₹50,000 and he had drawn ₹6,000 till his death. It is agreed that:

1. Goodwill is valued at two years' purchase of the average profit of the last three years: ₹1,10,000, ₹1,40,000 and ₹1,70,000. Qasim and Radha continue in their old ratio.
2. His share of profit till death is based on last year's profit.
3. Plant is revalued upwards by ₹12,000 and stock reduced by ₹7,000.
4. His executor is paid ₹69,500 at once; the remaining ₹1,00,000 is transferred to the executor's loan account.

Pass the journal entries.
questions.solution_md: Value goodwill first, record every adjustment to the date of death, then move the balance to the executor and settle it.

answer.model_answer_md:
Workings: average profit 1,40,000; goodwill = 2 × 1,40,000 = 2,80,000; Sanjay's share = 1/5 = 56,000. Profit till death = 1,70,000 × 3/12 × 1/5 = 8,500. Amount due = 1,00,000 + 10,000 + 1,000 + 56,000 + 8,500 − 6,000 = 1,69,500.
